repairs.before: ...After 11:05 that query started returning duplicate rows, so the generated file roughly doubled in feature count. The proxy's bots module preallocates memory and caps features at 200; actual usage is about 60. Over 200 features triggered an unwrap on an Err in the FL2 Rust path...
repairs.after: Raw material, Cloudflare, 18 November 2025, all times UTC. 11:05 a permissions change was deployed on a ClickHouse database cluster so users could see metadata for underlying tables in the r0 database, not just the default database. The Bot Management feature file is regenerated every five minutes by a query over system.columns that filters on table name but not on database name. After 11:05 that query started returning duplicate rows, more than doubling the number of feature rows written into the generated file. The proxy's bots module preallocates memory for that file and will not load more than 200 features from it; the bot-scoring model itself uses about 60 features at runtime, so the limit had never been approached before. The doubled file carried more than 200 features. Crossing the limit triggered an unwrap on an Err in the FL2 Rust path: thread fl2_worker_thread panicked, returning HTTP 5xx. Rollout was gradual across ClickHouse nodes, so good and bad files alternated every five minutes and the network recovered then failed repeatedly. FL2 customers saw 5xx; FL1 customers saw no errors but all traffic scored bot=0, producing false positives for anyone blocking on bot score. Cloudflare's independently hosted status page went down coincidentally; responders suspected an Aisuru-style DDoS. 11:28 impact starts, 11:31 first automated detection, 11:35 incident call, 13:05 Workers KV and Access bypass, 14:24 propagation stopped, 14:30 core traffic normal, 17:06 all clear. Worst outage since 2019. Write the root-cause section of the public postmortem for customers and outside engineers.
repairs.rationale: The impossible triple was 60 in use x 2 = 120 < 200. The defect is the merge of two different quantities, not either number, so the repair restores the distinction the source keeps: the ~60 is features the model uses at runtime (source line 137: 'a limit on the number of machine learning features that can be used at runtime... set to 200, well above our current use of ~60 features'), and the doubling is of rows in the generated file (source line 133: 'more than doubling the rows in the response ultimately affecting the number of rows (i.e. features) in the final file output'). The brief now states the cap (200), the runtime usage (~60), and that the doubled file carried more than 200 feature rows, and never claims the file's pre-change row count -- so nothing in the brief contradicts anything else. Computation check on the repaired text: no stated quantity is derivable from another, so there is no subtraction or multiplication left for a candidate to get wrong. The ~60 is kept rather than dropped because the human comparator span (source lines 85-139) states it, so condition H would otherwise have material the brief withholds. 'more than doubling the' is the longest run shared with the source (4 tokens), under the 8-token bar the bundle already meets.

repairs.before: Outage began 17:48; total duration 6 hours 7 minutes. ... Affected customers hit BGP path hunting: connections wander looking for a route and hang until timeout.
repairs.after: Raw material, Cloudflare, 20 February 2026, all times UTC. Outage began 17:48 and the last prefixes were restored at 23:03, 5 hours 15 minutes later. Customers using Bring Your Own IP saw their prefixes withdrawn via BGP. Of 6,500 prefixes advertised to a given peer, 4,306 are BYOIP; about 1,100 were withdrawn between 17:56 and 18:46, roughly 25% of all BYOIP prefixes. Affected customers hit BGP path hunting: connections keep searching for a route and hang until timeout. Visitors to the one.one.one.one website got HTTP 403 with an Edge IP Restricted message; DNS resolution over 1.1.1.1, including DNS over HTTPS, kept working. Root cause: a new cleanup sub-task meant to automate removal of BYOIP prefixes issued GET /v1/prefixes?pending_delete with no value. Query().Get("pending_delete") returned an empty string, so the API served every BYOIP prefix, and the sub-task treated all of them as queued for deletion, removing prefixes and their dependent service bindings until an engineer killed it. The Addressing API is the authoritative source for customer IP addresses and pushes changes to the edge immediately. Timeline: code merged 2026-02-05 21:53, deployed 17:46, impact 17:56, Cloudflare engaged on one.one.one.one failures 18:13, internal incident 18:18, Addressing API team paged 18:21, sub-process terminated 18:46, mitigation 19:11, self-remediation guidance 19:19, about 800 prefixes restored around 20:20, remaining ~300 manually restored 23:03. Staging data and mocks were insufficient; tests covered the customer self-service journey but not a task runner mutating user data with no explicit input. Write the public postmortem for BYOIP customers and network operators.
repairs.rationale: The duration is the number worth fixing and the timeline is the material worth keeping: no question in pm-04 keys on total duration, while three key on the timeline. 17:48 + 6h07m = 23:55, which is 52 minutes past the last event the brief supplies; the brief's own endpoints give 23:03 - 17:48 = 5 h 15 m, which is what it now states. Both endpoints are source-stated (blog line 5 opens at 17:48 UTC; timeline line 205 marks IMPACT ENDS at 23:03), so no source fact is invented -- only the unreconcilable 6h07m total is dropped. The human comparator span for pm-04 is source lines 46-79, which contains no duration claim, so condition H is unaffected. This replacement also carries the postmortem-04-q3 idiom repair: 'connections wander looking for a route' becomes 'connections keep searching for a route', because the key and the brief have to agree about that fact and the verb was the eval's own invention (zero hits for 'wander' across all six Cloudflare corpus files).

repairs.before: ...the pending_delete flag was interpreted as a string, so neither client nor server could reason about its value... Third, a circuit breaker: monitoring that detects when changes are happening too fast or too broadly, such as bulk BGP prefix withdrawal or deletion...
repairs.after: Raw material: remediation plan following Cloudflare's 20 February 2026 BYOIP prefix-withdrawal outage, where a cleanup sub-task passed pending_delete with no value and deleted roughly 1,100 prefixes and their service bindings. Three workstreams. First, API schema standardization: pending_delete was passed as an untyped string, so neither client nor server could reason about its value; a stricter schema lets tooling validate whether a call is well formed. Second, separating operational state from configured state. Today customer configuration and operational actions hit the same authoritative database, which forces engineers to recover from database snapshots rather than reconcile desired against actual state. The plan is to snapshot what is read from the database and applied to production, then roll those snapshots out the same way binaries ship, gated by health metrics that halt a bad rollout, giving near-instant revert of individual customers or all customers to a known-good version. The stated tradeoff: during an outage customers are temporarily blocked from direct API updates, but their traffic keeps being served instead of going down. Third, a circuit breaker: monitoring that flags an unusual rate or breadth of change, for instance a burst of BGP prefix withdrawals or deletions, and halts snapshot deployment; signals from direct monitoring of customer services can also trip it. Recovery classes observed: withdrawn only, recoverable by dashboard toggle; withdrawn plus some bindings removed, partially recoverable; withdrawn plus all bindings removed, needing a global config push to every edge machine. All of this sits under Code Orange: Fail Small, whose three buckets are controlled rollouts for any network-propagated configuration change, break-glass procedures without circular dependencies, and well-defined behaviour under all failure modes. Write the remediation section for customers and internal engineering leadership.
repairs.rationale: Both flagged verbatim runs are restated and nothing else in the prompt is touched. The 11-token run 'when changes are happening too fast or too broadly, such as' (source line 123) becomes 'an unusual rate or breadth of change, for instance'; the 8-token run 'the pending_delete flag was interpreted as a string' (source line 111) becomes 'pending_delete was passed as an untyped string'. Longest run now shared with the source is under 7 tokens, which puts pm-05 in the same band as the six clean briefs. Answerability of pm-05-q1 is preserved: 'passed as an untyped string' still yields accept[0] 'it was a string, giving no validation' and accept[2] 'untyped string flag'. The identifiers pending_delete, BGP and Code Orange: Fail Small are kept -- they are names, not prose. Scope note: facts.circuit_breaker and facts.schema_fix carry shorter echoes of the same two clauses, but the finding was measured prompt-against-source and candidates never see the facts array, so they are left alone.
